## Overview

The first step in learning Julia is making sure that the necessary software is installed and that the pieces can communicate. Visual Studio Code provides the interface where we will work, Julia executes the code, and the Julia extension connects Julia-specific features to VS Code.

This chapter installs each piece separately and verifies it before moving on. We will also become familiar with the parts of VS Code needed during setup, including the Command Palette and integrated terminal. Near the end of the chapter, we will start the Julia REPL and use a small calculation to confirm that Julia is ready to receive instructions.

**After working through this chapter, you will be able to:**

1. Distinguish VS Code, the Julia runtime, the Julia VS Code extension, the integrated terminal, the shell, and the Julia REPL.
2. Install VS Code on a Mac and locate the parts of its interface used during setup.
3. Install Julia with juliaup and verify that the shell can find and run it.
4. Install the official Julia VS Code extension and verify that its commands are available.
5. Start the integrated Julia REPL, evaluate a Julia expression, and inspect the installed Julia version.
6. Distinguish a `zsh` terminal session from a Julia REPL session and end both deliberately.

## Understand the software layers

The tools in this workflow have different responsibilities. Seeing Julia-related text or syntax coloring in an editor does not prove that the computer can execute Julia code. We will verify each layer by asking it to perform a small, observable task.

| Component | Role in the workflow | Evidence that it works |
|---|---|---|
| **VS Code** | Provides the interface for editing files, navigating folders, opening terminals, and using extensions. | The application opens and its main interface is visible. |
| **Julia runtime** | Reads and executes Julia instructions. | `julia --version` reports an installed version and Julia evaluates an expression. |
| **Julia VS Code extension** | Connects VS Code to the Julia runtime and adds Julia-aware commands, editing support, help, and an integrated Julia REPL. | `Julia: Start REPL` opens a working Julia session inside VS Code. |
| **Integrated terminal** | Provides a panel inside VS Code that can contain one or more terminal sessions. | The panel opens and displays a prompt. |
| **[Shell]{.glossary-term data-term="Shell"}** | Interprets operating-system commands inside a terminal session. On a current Mac, the default shell is usually `zsh`. | The prompt ends with `%` or `$`, and a command such as `julia --version` runs. |
| **Julia REPL** | Provides an interactive Julia session for entering expressions and immediately seeing their results. | The prompt says `julia>` and `6 * 7` returns `42`. |

If you know RStudio, these comparisons may help:

| Familiar RStudio feature | VS Code and Julia feature | Shared purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **R Console** | **Julia REPL** | Run language expressions interactively and retain values during the session. |
| **Terminal** | **`zsh` terminal session** | Run operating-system commands and launch programs. |
| **Files pane** | **Explorer** | Navigate folders and files. |
| **Source editor** | **VS Code editor** | Read and edit code stored in files. |

The Julia REPL is therefore similar to the R Console, even though VS Code displays it inside the terminal panel.

**Reflect:** VS Code is the interface, Julia is the language runtime, and an extension connects them. Installing one does not automatically establish that the others are present or correctly connected.

## Install Visual Studio Code

[Visual Studio Code (VS Code)]{.glossary-term data-term="Visual Studio Code (VS Code)"} is a code editor that can be extended to support different programming languages. These instructions use macOS on a Mac with Apple silicon. Readers using another operating system should follow the corresponding instructions on the official [VS Code download page](https://code.visualstudio.com/download).

**Goal:** Install VS Code in the Applications folder and open it successfully.

**Steps:**

1. Open the official [VS Code installation instructions for macOS](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/setup/mac).
2. Download the macOS version of VS Code. The Universal build supports both Intel-based Macs and Macs with Apple silicon; an Apple-silicon-specific build is also available.
3. Open the downloaded `.dmg` file.
4. Drag **Visual Studio Code.app** into the **Applications** folder.
5. Open the Applications folder and double-click **Visual Studio Code**.
6. If macOS asks whether you want to open an application downloaded from the internet, confirm only after verifying that the application came from the official VS Code website.

To keep VS Code in the Dock, Control-click its Dock icon and select **Options → Keep in Dock**.

**Check:** VS Code opens and displays a window containing its Activity Bar, editor area, and status bar. On a Mac, select **Code → About Visual Studio Code** to view the installed version.

**Reflect:** Installing VS Code provides the editor interface, but it does not install Julia. Julia must be installed separately before VS Code can run Julia code.

## Learn the VS Code controls used during setup

Only a few parts of the VS Code interface are needed during installation. We will return to the rest of the interface in the next chapter.

### Recognize the main areas

The vertical strip along the far-left edge is the [Activity Bar]{.glossary-term data-term="Activity Bar"}. Its icons open different views in the sidebar.

Select the [Explorer]{.glossary-term data-term="Explorer"} icon. The Explorer is used to navigate folders and files. It may be mostly empty when no project folder has been opened.

Select the [Extensions view]{.glossary-term data-term="Extensions View"}. An [extension]{.glossary-term data-term="Extension"} is an add-on that gives VS Code capabilities for a language or workflow. Later in this chapter, we will use this view to install Julia support.

Look along the bottom edge of the window. This is the [status bar]{.glossary-term data-term="Status Bar"}. The information displayed there changes according to the active file, folder, and installed extensions.

### Use the Command Palette

The [Command Palette]{.glossary-term data-term="Command Palette"} is a searchable menu of actions available in VS Code. It includes built-in commands and commands added by extensions.

Open it with **Shift–Command–P**, type part of a command’s name, and select the command you want. Press **Escape** to close it.

This chapter uses commands such as:

- `Developer: Reload Window`
- `Julia: Start REPL`

The Command Palette is useful when you know what action you need but do not know where it appears in the menus. VS Code’s [user-interface guide](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editing/userinterface#_command-palette) describes it as the main keyboard-accessible route to editor commands.

### Recognize terminal sessions

Open the [integrated terminal]{.glossary-term data-term="Integrated Terminal"} by selecting **Terminal → New Terminal**. The integrated terminal is the entire panel that opens near the bottom of VS Code. The panel can contain several independent [terminal sessions]{.glossary-term data-term="Terminal Session"} at the same time.

Look at the session list on the right side of the terminal panel. Each line represents one session and displays a name such as `zsh` or, after Julia is installed, `Julia REPL`.

1. Click a session name to display that session.
2. Click the **plus sign (`+`)** near the upper-right corner of the terminal panel to create another session.
3. Hover over an unneeded session and click its **trash-can** button to end and remove it.

Closing or hiding the terminal panel does not necessarily end the sessions inside it. VS Code can also restore terminal content after a window reload or application restart. If VS Code reports **History restored**, use the session name and current prompt—not old text higher in the panel—to determine which program is ready to receive an instruction. The [VS Code terminal guide](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/terminal/basics#_managing-terminals) documents the terminal list and session controls.

**Check:** Open **Terminal → New Terminal**. Find the new `zsh` entry in the session list, select it, and locate the prompt ending in `%` in the main terminal area.

**Reflect:** The terminal panel is a container. A terminal session is one running shell, REPL, or other process inside that container.

## Install Julia with juliaup

[Juliaup]{.glossary-term data-term="juliaup"} is Julia’s recommended installer and version manager. It installs a current stable Julia release and can later update Julia or switch among Julia versions. The current installation command is available from the official [Julia installation page](https://julialang.org/install/).

These instructions use the native Apple-silicon version of Julia.

**Goal:** Install the [Julia runtime]{.glossary-term data-term="Julia Runtime"} from an ordinary `zsh` terminal and verify that the shell can locate and launch it.

**Steps:**

1. Open a new integrated terminal in VS Code.
2. In the terminal-session list, select the session named `zsh`.
3. Confirm that the prompt ends with `%` and does not say `julia>`.
4. Check whether Julia is already available:

```bash
julia --version
```

If this command reports a Julia version, Julia is already installed and does not need to be installed again. Continue with the verification steps below.

If Julia is not installed, `zsh` will probably report `command not found: julia`. At the same ordinary shell prompt, enter the official installation command:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://install.julialang.org | sh
```

This command downloads the official juliaup installation script and passes it to the shell. Read the information displayed by the installer before accepting its proposed changes.

5. Follow the installer’s prompts and wait until it reports that Julia was successfully installed.
6. End the original terminal session with its trash-can button.
7. Open a fresh terminal with the **plus sign (`+`)** so the new `zsh` session loads the updated [PATH]{.glossary-term data-term="PATH"}.
8. Run these commands one at a time:

```bash
juliaup status
julia --version
```

`juliaup status` should list an installed Julia channel. `julia --version` should report the installed Julia version.

9. Verify that the Julia build matches the Mac’s Apple-silicon architecture:

```bash
julia -e 'println(Sys.ARCH)'
```

**Check:** The final command should print:

```text
aarch64
```

It should then return to the ordinary shell prompt. The `-e` option started Julia, evaluated one expression, printed the result, and exited without opening an interactive REPL.

**Reflect:** These checks establish that Julia is installed, that the shell can find it through the command path, and that the native Apple-silicon build can run. Syntax highlighting alone would not establish any of those facts.

## Install the Julia VS Code extension

The [Julia VS Code extension]{.glossary-term data-term="Julia VS Code Extension"} connects VS Code to the installed Julia runtime. It adds Julia-aware commands, syntax support, code completion, documentation, and an integrated Julia REPL. The extension does not include or replace Julia itself.

**Goal:** Install the official Julia extension and verify that its commands are available.

**Steps:**

1. Open the **Extensions** view from the Activity Bar.
2. Search for `Julia`.
3. Select the extension with all four of these identifying details:

    - **Name:** Julia
    - **Description:** Julia Language Support
    - **Publisher:** julialang, with a verified-publisher checkmark
    - **Identifier:** `julialang.language-julia`

    “Julia Language Support” is the description, not the extension’s identifier. To locate the identifier, open the extension’s details page and look in the extension information or **More Info** area.

4. Select **Install**.

The official [Julia extension setup guide](https://www.julia-vscode.org/docs/stable/setup/) explains that the extension normally detects Julia automatically when the Julia executable is available on the system command path.

### Reload or restart VS Code

Reload VS Code after installing the extension:

1. Open the Command Palette with **Shift–Command–P**.
2. Search for `Developer: Reload Window`.
3. Select the command.

Reloading the window restarts the VS Code interface and its extensions without quitting the entire application.

If reloading does not resolve an extension or command-path problem, completely quit VS Code with **Command–Q**, then reopen it. Clicking the red window button may close the window without quitting the application.

When VS Code or Julia first starts an integrated process, macOS may display a permission request. Read the request and approve it only when it clearly corresponds to the action you just initiated. If the requested access is unexpected, pause and investigate before approving it.

**Check:** In the Extensions view, the Julia extension should display **Installed** or offer controls to disable or uninstall it. Open the Command Palette and enter `Julia:`. The command `Julia: Start REPL` should appear.

**Reflect:** The presence of Julia commands verifies that the extension is installed and enabled. Starting the REPL successfully will provide stronger evidence that the extension found the Julia runtime.

## Start and verify the Julia REPL

The [Julia REPL]{.glossary-term data-term="Julia REPL"} is an interactive Julia session. REPL stands for *Read–Eval–Print Loop*: Julia reads an expression, evaluates it, prints the result, and waits for another expression.

Starting Julia by typing `julia` at an ordinary shell prompt also creates a Julia REPL. However, the REPL started with the extension’s `Julia: Start REPL` command includes additional VS Code integration. The official [Julia extension documentation](https://www.julia-vscode.org/docs/stable/userguide/runningcode/) recommends using that command for interactive work in VS Code.

**Goal:** Demonstrate that the Julia extension located the installed Julia runtime and can start an integrated session.

**Steps:**

1. Open the Command Palette with **Shift–Command–P**.
2. Enter `Julia: Start REPL`.
3. Select the command and allow Julia time to start.
4. Look at the terminal-session list.
5. Select the new Julia session and confirm that the main terminal area contains a Julia banner and a `julia>` prompt.
6. At the `julia>` prompt, enter:

```julia
6 * 7
```

7. Press **Return**.
8. At the next `julia>` prompt, enter:

```julia
versioninfo()
```

**Check:** The first expression should return:

```text
42
```

`versioninfo()` should report the Julia version and system information. On a Mac with Apple silicon, the report should identify the machine architecture as ARM or `aarch64`. The prompt should return to `julia>` after each expression.

**Reflect:** This test establishes more than successful installation. The `Julia: Start REPL` command came from the extension, the extension found the Julia runtime, and the runtime evaluated Julia code. The Julia REPL is serving the role that the Console serves in RStudio.

## Distinguish the shell from the Julia REPL

Julia expressions and shell commands must go to the program that understands them. VS Code can keep a shell and a Julia REPL available as separate terminal sessions.

1. Leave the Julia REPL running.
2. Click the **plus sign (`+`)** in the terminal panel to create another terminal.
3. Find the new [`zsh`]{.glossary-term data-term="zsh"} entry in the terminal-session list.
4. Toggle between `zsh` and the Julia session by selecting their names.

Use the prompts as evidence:

- Enter Julia expressions such as `6 * 7` or `versioninfo()` at `julia>`.
- Enter shell commands such as `julia --version` at the prompt ending in `%`.
- Do not copy either prompt as part of a command.

The visible prompts will resemble:

```text
zsh session:    your-name@computer-name ~ %
Julia session:  julia>
```

If several old `zsh` sessions appear, keep one ordinary shell session and use the trash-can buttons to end the extras.

**Check:** The terminal-session list contains at least one Julia session and one `zsh` session. Selecting each displays a different prompt.

**Reflect:** The terminal panel can hold several sessions. Switching sessions is analogous to moving between RStudio’s Console and Terminal panes, even though VS Code places both sessions in one panel.

## End the sessions deliberately

A running session can retain values or continue using computer resources until it is stopped.

1. Select the Julia REPL session.
2. At `julia>`, enter:

```julia
exit()
```

The `julia>` prompt should disappear. Depending on how the extension created the session, the terminal may close or return control to a shell.

3. Select an ordinary `zsh` session that is no longer needed.
4. Enter:

```bash
exit
```

You can also use the trash-can button to end and remove a terminal session.

**Check:** The ended sessions no longer display an active `julia>` or `%` prompt waiting for input.

**Reflect:** Hiding the terminal panel, stopping a running program, and removing a terminal session are different actions. Ending sessions deliberately makes their state visible.

## Diagnose common setup problems

A failed check identifies which layer requires attention. It does not mean that the entire installation must be repeated.

- If VS Code does not open after downloading, confirm that **Visual Studio Code.app** was moved into the Applications folder and that it came from the official VS Code website.

- If `julia --version` returns `command not found`, end the existing `zsh` session and open a fresh one. If the problem remains, check whether `juliaup status` works and review the juliaup installer’s completion message.

- If the Julia extension is difficult to identify, open its details and verify the name **Julia**, description **Julia Language Support**, verified publisher **julialang**, and identifier `julialang.language-julia`.

- If `Julia: Start REPL` is absent from the Command Palette, confirm that the Julia extension is installed and enabled. Then run `Developer: Reload Window`.

- If `julia --version` works in a new terminal but the extension cannot find Julia, completely quit VS Code with **Command–Q** and reopen it. If automatic detection still fails, run `which julia` in `zsh` and use the returned executable location for the extension’s `julia.executablePath` setting.

- If macOS displays a permission request immediately after an action you initiated, read the request and confirm that it names the expected application, folder, or process. Do not approve an unrelated or unexplained request merely to continue.

- If several `zsh` entries appear, they are separate terminal sessions. Select each from the terminal list, retain the one you need, and remove extras with their trash-can buttons.

- If Julia syntax is highlighted but no expression has run successfully, continue verification. Highlighting confirms language recognition, not the presence of a working runtime.

- If `Sys.ARCH` does not report `aarch64` on a Mac with Apple silicon, review the Julia installation before proceeding.

## Summary

In this chapter, you installed and opened VS Code, installed Julia with juliaup, and installed the Julia VS Code extension. You used the Command Palette and integrated terminal, distinguished the terminal panel from the sessions inside it, and verified the Julia installation from an ordinary `zsh` shell. You then started the integrated Julia REPL, evaluated `6 * 7`, inspected the installed Julia version, and ended the Julia and shell sessions deliberately. These checks provide observable evidence that VS Code, the Julia extension, and the Julia runtime are installed and communicating.

## Chapter Terms {#chapter-terms}

**Activity Bar**: The vertical group of icons used to switch among major VS Code views.

**Command Palette**: VS Code’s searchable menu of built-in and extension-provided actions. On a Mac, open it with **Shift–Command–P**.

**Explorer**: VS Code’s file-navigation view for opening, creating, renaming, and organizing folders and files.

**Extension**: An add-on that expands VS Code’s capabilities. An extension can connect the editor to other installed software but does not replace that software.

**Extensions View**: The VS Code view used to search for, install, inspect, enable, and remove extensions.

**Integrated Terminal**: The terminal panel built into VS Code. It can contain multiple terminal sessions.

**Julia REPL**: Julia’s interactive Read–Eval–Print Loop, which reads an expression, evaluates it, prints the result, and waits for another instruction. It is roughly analogous to the R Console in RStudio.

**Julia Runtime**: The installed software that interprets and executes Julia code.

**Julia VS Code Extension**: The extension that connects VS Code to the Julia runtime and provides Julia-aware commands, code completion, help, and an integrated REPL.

**juliaup**: Julia’s recommended installer and version manager for installing, updating, and selecting Julia versions.

**PATH**: A list of directories the shell searches when locating an executable command such as `julia`.

**Shell**: A command interpreter that runs inside a terminal session and accepts operating-system commands.

**Status Bar**: The area at the bottom of VS Code that displays information about the current context.

**Terminal Session**: One running shell, REPL, task, or other program listed inside VS Code’s integrated terminal panel.

**Visual Studio Code (VS Code)**: A general-purpose code editor that can be extended to support different programming languages and workflows.

**zsh**: The default shell on current versions of macOS. It accepts operating-system commands at a prompt that usually ends with `%`.
